title: How Cachaça Is Made
subtitle: Fresh sugarcane juice, a copper still, and the one difference that separates it from rum.
description: A B1 reading and listening text on cachaça — how it is produced, what makes it different from rum, and what distinguishes a good bottle — with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: Cachaça is a Brazilian spirit distilled from sugarcane, and it is the base of the caipirinha. It is often described as a kind of rum, which is close enough to be useful and wrong in one important respect. Most rum is made from molasses, the thick dark syrup left over once sugar has been crystallised out of the cane juice. Cachaça is made from the fresh juice itself, pressed and fermented within hours of cutting. That single difference is why the two taste as unlike each other as they do: cachaça keeps a grassy, vegetal quality that molasses-based spirits lose.

The process has four stages, and the first is the one with the tightest deadline. The cane is cut and crushed, and the juice is filtered. From the moment the cane is cut it begins to deteriorate, so a serious producer presses within a day. The juice is then fermented in tanks for anything from a day to a few days, with yeast converting the sugar into alcohol. Some distilleries use commercial yeast for consistency; others use strains they have cultivated on the farm for generations, which is one of the things that makes a producer's cachaça taste like theirs and nobody else's.

Third comes distillation, traditionally in copper pot stills. Copper is not decorative: it reacts with sulphur compounds produced during fermentation and removes flavours that would otherwise be unpleasant. The distiller separates the run into three parts — the head, the heart and the tail — and keeps only the heart. The head contains volatile compounds that come off first and taste harsh; the tail turns heavy and oily. Deciding exactly where to make each cut is the distiller's central skill, and it cannot be automated in a small operation because it is done by smell and taste.

The fourth stage, ageing, is optional, and it is where cachaça becomes genuinely distinctive. Unaged cachaça — branca, white — is bottled straight away and tastes of the cane: fresh, grassy, a little sharp. Aged cachaça is rested in wooden barrels for months or years. Brazilian producers use oak, as the rest of the spirits world does, but they also use native woods that almost nobody else has access to: amburana, which gives a warm, spiced character close to cinnamon and vanilla; jequitibá rosa, which is much more neutral and lets the cane show through; balsam and others. A row of the same spirit aged in five different woods will produce five recognisably different drinks.

What separates a good bottle from a poor one comes down to a few things. Cane cut at the right ripeness and pressed quickly. A controlled fermentation rather than a rushed one. A careful cut during distillation, which is what removes the harshness people associate with cheap cachaça. And, if it has been aged, decent barrels and enough patience.

As for how to drink it, the caipirinha — cachaça, lime, sugar, ice — is made with branca, and a good branca improves it considerably more than most people expect. Aged cachaça is generally drunk on its own, at room temperature, the way you would drink a whisky. Using a well-aged bottle in a cocktail is not an error exactly, but you will be paying for wood character that the lime then covers up.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Answer from the sense of the process being described.

items.prompt: What is the essential difference between cachaça and most rum?
options: Cachaça is made from fresh cane juice; most rum is made from molasses
Cachaça is distilled twice and rum only once
items.explanation: “That single difference is why the two taste as unlike each other as they do.”

items.prompt: Why must the cane be pressed quickly after cutting?
options: Because it attracts insects once cut
Because it begins to deteriorate from the moment it is cut
Because the juice ferments on its own within hours
items.explanation: “A serious producer presses within a day” — this is the stage with the tightest deadline.

items.prompt: Why do some distilleries use their own yeast strains?
options: Because commercial yeast is unavailable in Brazil
Because it gives their cachaça a character no one else's has
items.explanation: Commercial yeast is used for consistency; farm strains are used for distinctiveness. The text gives both reasons.

items.prompt: Why is copper used for the stills?
options: It reacts with sulphur compounds and removes unpleasant flavours
It conducts heat more evenly than steel
It is traditional but has no practical effect
items.explanation: “Copper is not decorative” — the text goes out of its way to say the choice is chemical, not aesthetic.

items.prompt: What does the distiller keep from the run?
items.explanation: The head is harsh and volatile; the tail is heavy and oily. Only the heart is kept.

items.prompt: Why can't the cut be automated in a small distillery?
options: Because the equipment is too old
Because it is judged by smell and taste
Because the law requires a person to do it
items.explanation: The text calls it “the distiller's central skill” for exactly that reason.

items.prompt: What effect does amburana have compared with jequitibá rosa?
options: Amburana gives warm, spiced flavours; jequitibá rosa is neutral and lets the cane show
Amburana is neutral; jequitibá rosa adds vanilla
items.explanation: Which is the point of the sentence that follows: five woods produce five recognisably different drinks.

items.prompt: What does the writer advise about using aged cachaça in a caipirinha?
options: That it is a mistake and ruins the cocktail
That it is the traditional way to make one
That you will be paying for wood character the lime then hides
items.explanation: “Not an error exactly” — the objection is about waste, not correctness.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: All cachaça is aged in wood.
items.explanation: False — ageing is optional. Branca is bottled straight away.
True — unaged, it “tastes of the cane: fresh, grassy, a little sharp”.

items.statement: Brazilian producers use only native woods.
items.explanation: False — they use oak as well, “as the rest of the spirits world does”.
False — “from a day to a few days”.

items.statement: A careful cut during distillation removes harshness.
items.explanation: True — it is named as “what removes the harshness people associate with cheap cachaça”.

items.statement: A caipirinha is traditionally made with branca.
items.explanation: True — and the text adds that a good branca improves it more than people expect.

exercises.title: The Vocabulary of Production
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the right word. These terms apply to whisky, rum and brandy just as well.

items.prompt: The juice is ___ for two days before it is distilled.
items.explanation: Fermentation is the stage where yeast converts sugar into alcohol; distillation then concentrates it.

items.prompt: Cut cane begins to ___ within hours.
items.explanation: To deteriorate is to get worse in quality.

items.prompt: The spirit is ___ in oak ___ for three years.
items.explanation: Ageing happens in barrels; a still is where distillation happens.

items.prompt: The distiller makes the ___ by smell rather than by measurement.
items.explanation: The cut is the point at which the distiller stops collecting one part of the run.

items.prompt: They use a yeast ___ they have ___ on the farm for generations.
items.explanation: A strain is a particular variety of a microorganism; to cultivate is to grow and maintain it deliberately.

items.prompt: Amburana and jequitibá rosa are ___ Brazilian woods.
items.explanation: Native means originating naturally in a particular country — which is why other countries' distillers cannot easily use them.

discussion: The text says the distiller's central skill cannot be automated. What other jobs depend on judgement that a machine cannot make?
Cachaça is often called “Brazilian rum”. Is a rough comparison helpful when introducing something, or does it get in the way?
Five woods produce five different drinks from the same spirit. Does that make the wood or the spirit the more important ingredient?
Is there a product from your country that outsiders regularly misunderstand or mislabel?
Write about 120 words describing how something traditional from your country is made, using the stages of the process in order.
